newsitem.title: INDIA: Fractious Indian government seen weaker but safe.
newsitem.headline: Fractious Indian government seen weaker but safe.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's two-month-old government appears to be in no immediate danger despite an impending split in his party, riven by factional bickering, political analysts said on Friday.
But a newly weakened Janata Dal party might embolden its powerful ally the Congress party, which is waiting impatiently in the wings to grab a centre stage position.
The rift within the Janata Dal emerged after the group was forced to hold internal elections for a new president, which pitted chief Laloo Prasad Yadav against another leader.

Yadav's supporters said the voter's list was rigged to favour his rival and boycotted the poll. They have vowed to hold a parallel election to ensure Yadav's victory, pushing the deeply divided party towards a debilitating split.
"Obviously, Janata Dal leaders consider death wish to be their birthright," the Hindustan Times remarked in an editorial.

The group is the largest in Gujral's 13-party centre-left government, which also leans heavily on Congress support in parliament for its survival. Yadav on Thursday said his supporters would continue to back the administration.
There are two parties which are not in the government but participate in Gujral's 15-party United Front alliance.

Pran Chopra, political analyst at New Delhi's Centre for Policy Research, said Gujral could rest easy because both Congress and Janata Dal were keen to avoid mid-term polls, likely to favour the main opposition Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) the most.

"The probability is that such party as Mr Laloo Prasad Yadav may form will become either another constituent of the United Front or will take the position of supporting the government without joining it," Chopra said.
"So instead of 13 parties, there will be 14," he said.

"But there is no gainsaying the image of the government, its effectiveness has taken a knock that does not give the United Front the kind of platform it would want to contest the next election on," Chopra told Reuters.

The alliance is already locked in a long-running divisive controversy over raising oil prices -- essential to contain a mounting subsidy bill but opposed by communist partners because it will stoke inflation and hurt the poor.
BJP president Lal Krishna Advani said Congress would swiftly launch a bid for power, just months after it toppled a previous United Front government by abruptly withdrawing support.

"I can foresee Congress making yet another bid to grab power in Delhi no sooner than there is a split in the Janata Dal. Last time they tried it in April but failed and decided to let the United Front continue," Advani told reporters.

"The instability of the central government in Delhi is largely on account of the incongruous arrangement between them and Congress. Despite being the larger party, Congress is extending support to it from outside," he said.
News reports quoted Congress leaders exhorting party cadres to prepare for mid-term polls.
"Coalition governments are weak and unstable, and some parties are disintegrating," Congress spokesman Vithal Gadgil told Reuters.
"The split will obviously have an impact on the prime minister's authority. We will continue to support them. Let us see how the situation develops," Gadgil added.
Gujral's reputation for honesty has been tarnished by a federal police decision to indict Yadav in a $280-million embezzlement scandal over animal welfare funds in the northern state of Bihar.
Yadav, who is also Bihar's chief minister, says he is innocent and has refused to resign from either post.

In a move that drew sharp criticism from even coalition constituents, the government announced on Monday it was removing the director of the Central Bureau of Investigation who had spearheaded probes into the scandal.

"The future of the Gujral government comes under a question mark despite the assurances of Mr Yadav's supporters that the splinter party would continue to support the central government," the Hindustan Times said. "Such support is bound to carry a price tag."
